glossary.union proposal: The union brought a new article to the table for the first time. Harvard hasn't yet responded.
glossary.union counter: The union responded to Harvard's previous proposal with revised language. The article is in active back-and-forth.
glossary.union counter-proposal: Same as a union counter. The union revised its position in response to Harvard.
glossary.union package proposal: The union brought this article as part of a bundle of articles all proposed together. Often a strategic move to push multiple things forward at once.
glossary.union package: Same as union package proposal. Article was bundled with others.
glossary.union package proposal (withdraw): The union strategically withdrew this article from negotiation. Usually done to concentrate pressure on the most important fights.
glossary.union re-assertion: The union restated its previous proposal without changing the language, signaling to Harvard that the position stands.
glossary.union reassertion: The union restated its previous proposal without changing the language, signaling to Harvard that the position stands.
glossary.harvard proposal: Harvard brought a new article to the table for the first time.
glossary.harvard counter: Harvard responded to the union's previous proposal with revised language.
glossary.harvard counter-proposal: Same as a Harvard counter. Harvard revised its position in response to the union.
glossary.harvard package: Harvard brought this article as part of a bundle of articles proposed together.
glossary.harvard rejection: Harvard formally said no to the union's proposal without offering an alternative.
glossary.harvard rejection (no counter): Harvard formally said no to the union's proposal without offering an alternative. The article is stuck unless the union proposes again.
glossary.harvard reassertion: Harvard did not change their position. They restated what they had already proposed on the date noted. Usually a stalling move with no movement at the table.
glossary.university proposal: Harvard brought a new article to the table for the first time.
glossary.university counter: Harvard responded to the union's previous proposal with revised language.
glossary.university counter-proposal: Same as a Harvard counter. Harvard revised its position in response to the union.
glossary.ta: Tentative Agreement. Both sides agreed to the article's language at the table. Locked in pending full contract ratification by members at the end of bargaining.
glossary.tentative agreement: Both sides agreed to the article's language at the table. Locked in pending full contract ratification by members at the end of bargaining.
glossary.moved to article 4: This article was folded into Article 4 (Employment Appointment Security) rather than negotiated separately.

articles.name: Ground Rules
articles.unionAsks: Open bargaining (members allowed to observe in person and over Zoom). Enforceable protections against ICE/DHS during sessions: key-card access to the bargaining room, advance notification if federal agents arrive on campus. Accessibility accommodations.
articles.harvardPosition: Rejected open bargaining repeatedly. Argued that observers would create a 'chilling effect.' Refused to lock the bargaining room door or commit to ICE protections, directing the union to existing Office of General Counsel guidelines that don't materially protect against detention. Accepted one specific disability accommodation.

articles.name: Titles and Classifications
articles.unionAsks: Limited public detail.
articles.harvardPosition: Included in Harvard's 5/14 full-contract package.

articles.name: Employment Appointment Letter
articles.unionAsks: Timely appointment letters that include the basic info workers need: department/program, tax rate, funding source. So people aren't left without paychecks when admin systems lag. Accountability when letters arrive late.
articles.harvardPosition: Added a line that pay is 'taxable income' but refused to fix the late-letter problem. Called the union's information requirements 'cumbersome and onerous.' Blames individual departments and programs for delays rather than committing to systemic accountability.

articles.name: Employment Appointment Security
articles.unionAsks: Full pay for TFs whose sections are canceled. At least two weeks' notice if that happens. Protections for RAs whose appointments are cut. As of February 2026, this article also absorbed the Lab Transition Program: six months of guaranteed funding, tuition, healthcare, and benefits for RAs leaving unsafe, abusive, or broken advising relationships (modeled on MIT's program).
articles.harvardPosition: Argued the union's appointment-security proposal 'did a disservice to prior efforts' because the union disagreed with Harvard's reading of who's eligible for security pay. Has not engaged meaningfully with the lab transition program component.

articles.name: Job Posting
articles.unionAsks: Protections and agreements around job postings for in-unit positions: transparency about available work and fair access.
articles.harvardPosition: Initial proposal from fall 2025. Limited public detail.

articles.name: Grievance and Arbitration
articles.unionAsks: Realistic timeline for filing grievances: initially 90 business days (roughly one semester), narrowed in negotiation to 45. Codified privacy protections for workers who file grievances. Strong anti-retaliation language with a clear, usable definition of retaliation.
articles.harvardPosition: Started at 30 days for filing, moved to 35 (an extra five days). Refused to codify acceptance of late grievances, claiming extensions could be granted on a case-by-case basis through 'mutual agreement.' Rejected the union's definition of retaliation as 'too broad' and 'outside their control.' Resisted codifying privacy protections.

articles.name: Non-Discrimination, Harassment, and Abuse
articles.unionAsks: Codified identity-specific protections (race, color, religion, caste, creed, sex, sexual orientation, etc.) that exist in the current contract. 'Real Recourse': access to the union grievance process as an option in addition to Harvard's internal process, so survivors can choose. Anti-retaliation language. Right to union representation in meetings. (1 in 5 student workers have experienced harassment, discrimination, or bullying in their workplace.)
articles.harvardPosition: Removed identity-specific protections from contract language; defers to University-wide policy that Harvard can amend at any time without union input. Refuses union grievance access (survivors get only the internal process Harvard fully controls). Initially stripped out the right to union representation in meetings. Added 'or retaliation' phrasing as a minor concession. Cited that roughly 10% of complaints being dismissed is 'negligible.' On 5/14, Harvard said they were considering the union's proposal to allow grievances for remedies in Title IX, discrimination, and harassment cases, and looking into the legal details.

articles.name: Academic Retaliation
articles.unionAsks: Explicit protections against academic retaliation from faculty mentors and advisors: bad rec letters, denied professional opportunities, blocked academic progress. Other graduate union contracts protect against academic retaliation; Harvard's does not.
articles.harvardPosition: Says current internal mechanisms are sufficient. Initially questioned why a neutral, non-University-run process is needed when Harvard has its own. At one session asked how the union knows the current process isn't working given 'very little use.' Union response: reporting misconduct to a board of the accused's colleagues suppresses reporting.

articles.name: Intellectual Property, Scholarly and Research Misconduct
articles.unionAsks: Student worker rights to intellectual property they produce. Clear dispute resolution processes for research misconduct disputes.
articles.harvardPosition: Proposed cuts to existing IP protections from the previous contract. Resisted union's clarifying questions.

articles.name: Health and Safety
articles.unionAsks: Stronger and clearer timelines for disability accommodations. Safer approach to 'wellness checks' that doesn't default to armed police response. Protection against involuntary police entry into non-public spaces where workers live and work. Real accountability around accommodations data.
articles.harvardPosition: Says enforceable timelines would be 'difficult.' Has not provided requested data on denied accommodation requests or informal resolutions. Director of Disability Resources briefed the union but said the data wasn't 'readily available.'

articles.name: Training
articles.unionAsks: Rights to workplace-related trainings. Limited public detail on specific disputes.
articles.harvardPosition: Harvard's initial proposal in fall 2025.

articles.name: Non-Citizen Student Worker Rights
articles.unionAsks: Comprehensive legal assistance in the event of detention or federal immigration enforcement. Expanded leave provisions and remote-work provisions for immigration-related proceedings. Protections against federal presence on campus. Limits on the University sharing student worker records with federal agencies.
articles.harvardPosition: Ghosted the union for 9+ months without responding (June 2025 to February 2026). Eventually said protections against ICE would interfere with Harvard's 'relationship with the federal government,' though peer universities including Yale, the University of California system, and WPI have passed similar ICE-off-campus language. Refused to release roughly $400K from the existing legal defense fund. As of 5/14, no movement on the union's immigration leave proposal, even though Harvard implemented a similar policy during COVID for workers detained or stranded abroad.

articles.name: Workspace and Materials
articles.unionAsks: Available private space for student workers to hold office hours, supervisor meetings, etc., reasonably close to the workplace.
articles.harvardPosition: Initially resisted, then agreed. TA reached 2/2/2026 — first TA of the bargaining cycle.

articles.name: Workload
articles.unionAsks: Protections against unpaid teaching labor (workers performing the same job as paid peers without pay). Accountability around appointment-period workloads. Limits on workload increases without compensation.
articles.harvardPosition: Did not engage meaningfully. Article was strategically withdrawn by the union on 5/14/2026 as part of broader package negotiations.

articles.name: Union Access and Rights
articles.unionAsks: Information about workers in the unit (Harvard has invoked FERPA to obstruct this, including treating pay rates as 'educational records'). Union representation in worker orientations. Dedicated, ADA-compliant union workspaces across campuses. Paid union leadership positions (executive board members currently volunteer uncompensated).
articles.harvardPosition: Resists information sharing on FERPA grounds. Not engaging substantively on workspace or paid positions. Harvard's 5/14 package would also reduce union access to worker orientations.

articles.name: Discipline and Discharge
articles.unionAsks: Just cause for discipline. Full due process. Clear union representation rights. No discipline without an investigation.
articles.harvardPosition: Proposed a faster, weaker process where the University can discipline workers without any investigation, forcing workers to fight discipline after it's already been imposed. Harvard's 5/14 package would further erode fair processes for discipline and discharge.

articles.name: Compensation
articles.unionAsks: $55,000 base salary (up from $49,998). $25/hour floor for hourly workers (up from $21.50). Automatic annual increases of 5% or inflation, whichever is higher. Pay equity between TFs and RAs — TFs after the G4 year in many humanities and social sciences departments currently make only ~$26,000 for teaching the standard load.
articles.harvardPosition: The 5/14 package offers raises of 1% per year rising to 11% from 10% over a 4-year contract, averaging 2.75% per year, well below inflation. Hourly workers offered $0.50/year. Many TFs would still qualify for SNAP food benefits through 2029. Harvard offered $1 million more in compensation while the endowment grew by $3.7 billion in the same period; their lead negotiator called the proposal 'generous.' Told the bargaining committee in March that TFs needing more money should 'look into getting jobs in the summer' and 'work 4-5 sections.' On pay equity, when asked at the 5/14 session why Harvard TFs are paid nearly 60% less than TFs at MIT, a top GSAS administrator responded: 'Maybe TFs at MIT work more.'

articles.name: Health and Dental Insurance
articles.unionAsks: Full dental coverage. Expanded healthcare fund. Continued access to healthcare during leaves of absence (critical for workers on medical leave who currently lose coverage at the worst time).
articles.harvardPosition: Limited engagement until 5/14. Harvard's 5/14 package would eliminate the union-administered healthcare fund and remove guaranteed health insurance during medical leaves, both of which are critical protections in the current contract.

articles.name: Childcare Fund
articles.unionAsks: Continuation of the prior $16,000-per-child coverage.
articles.harvardPosition: $6,500/year per child. For context: Harvard's own campus childcare facilities charge $3,780/month, so the offered fund covers less than two months of Harvard's own program. The proposed childcare benefit also moves from union-administered to University-administered, with no contractual obligation to pay out a single penny. Harvard's 5/14 package would eliminate the union-administered childcare benefit entirely, alongside healthcare, emergency funds, dental, legal expense, non-citizen worker assistance, and dependent premiums.

articles.name: Hourly SW Access to Benefit Pools
articles.unionAsks: Hourly student workers should have full access to benefit funds, currently blocked. Eligibility should not depend on appointment type.
articles.harvardPosition: Continued exclusion.

articles.name: Legal Expense Fund
articles.unionAsks: Expanded legal expense fund with explicit coverage for urgent immigration representation. Release of the ~$400K already owed under the existing contract that Harvard has failed to make accessible.
articles.harvardPosition: Proposed replacing the union-administered legal fund with a subsidized MetLife legal services plan. The MetLife plan explicitly does NOT cover urgent immigration representation (rapid response when work authorization is at risk). Also appears not to cover Title IX representation. Refused to engage with the existing $400K issue, calling it 'not relevant.' Harvard's 5/14 package would eliminate the union-administered legal expense fund entirely.

articles.name: Leave Provisions
articles.unionAsks: 12 weeks of paid family and medical leave. Healthcare coverage continued during leaves (so no one loses insurance during a medical crisis). Retained student status during medical leave. 'Placeholder' credits that let workers on leave maintain enrollment.
articles.harvardPosition: Rejected paid family/medical leave. Rejected continued healthcare during leaves. Rejected placeholder credits, claiming they would 'reward' students not making academic progress.

articles.name: Holidays, Personal Days, Vacation
articles.unionAsks: Spring break leave for student workers. Required notice that workers are entitled to personal time and holidays. Expanded eligibility to include hourly workers. One vacation day per month for TFs.
articles.harvardPosition: Initially dismissive, implying TFs' schedules were already 'flexible' enough. Reached tentative agreement on 4/9/2026 — second TA of the bargaining cycle.

articles.name: Emergency Grant
articles.unionAsks: Expanded emergency grant fund. Clear and accessible application/distribution process.
articles.harvardPosition: No substantive counter through early 2026. Harvard's 5/14 package would eliminate the union-administered emergency fund entirely, alongside healthcare, childcare, dental, legal expense, non-citizen worker assistance, and dependent premiums.

articles.name: Union Security
articles.unionAsks: Agency shop / 'fair-share' arrangement — everyone who benefits from the contract contributes via dues or an equivalent fee. Standard across most graduate union contracts. Already in place for other Harvard unions (HUCTW).
articles.harvardPosition: Resists fair-share arrangements. Argues graduate workers are 'different' because they enter as students. Wants to maintain current open-shop structure where many workers benefit from the contract without contributing to union finances. Harvard's 5/14 package would eliminate fair-share fees outright.

articles.name: Academic Freedom
articles.unionAsks: Academic freedom protections on matters relevant to the subject and purpose of the worker's appointment. Other graduate union contracts include this; Harvard's does not.
articles.harvardPosition: Rejected without offering a counter. Doesn't want real language on this issue, even though it directly affects student workers' jobs.

articles.name: Lab Transition Program
articles.unionAsks: Six months of guaranteed funding, tuition, healthcare, and full benefits for salaried RAs leaving unsafe, abusive, or broken advising relationships. Modeled on MIT's Guaranteed Transitional Support program.
articles.harvardPosition: Did not respond as a standalone proposal. The union folded this into Article 4 (Appointment Security) on 4/13/2026.

articles.name: Accessible Transit
articles.unionAsks: Guaranteed accessible transportation for student workers with disability accommodations via the Daytime Van Service. Expanded to both daytime and evening service across all Harvard campuses. Ride-share coverage when van wait times exceed 30 minutes.
articles.harvardPosition: No real engagement yet.

articles.name: Fund Access
articles.unionAsks: Workers retain control and bargained-for access to benefit funds. Maintain union-administered benefit structure with clear rules.
articles.harvardPosition: Eliminate union-administered benefit funds entirely. Replace with a University-administered program (much of which already exists as extracontractual programs Harvard repackaged as if they were won at the table). Under Harvard's proposal, the University would not be contractually obligated to pay out a single penny. Disputes excluded from grievance. Approximately 1,000 workers would be excluded altogether: hourly workers, many Master's students, and DDes, EdLD, DrPH, and SJD candidates.

articles.name: Benefit Fund Rules
articles.unionAsks: Rules for application and distribution of benefit funds across the contract: eligibility, timelines, appeals process, transparency.
articles.harvardPosition: Wants discretion to administer funds without bargained rules.

articles.name: Benefits Trust
articles.unionAsks: Shift management of benefit funds from the union to an independent trust, reducing administrative burden for both parties.
articles.harvardPosition: No counter on record.

articles.name: Notice of Non-Retaliation
articles.unionAsks: New article introduced 5/14/2026. Codifies advance notice of non-retaliation as a separate protection. Detailed proposal language not yet public.
articles.harvardPosition: No response yet.

sessions.title: Session #23: After 2 weeks of strikes, Harvard offers less than nothing
sessions.tldr: Harvard's 'package' proposal would revert 11 open articles to old contract language and force union concessions on 16 articles. In exchange: a 1% raise rising to 11% over 4 years (averaging 2.75%/year, well below inflation). Bargaining committee secured another session for 5/21.

articleSummaries.20: After two-plus weeks of strikes, Harvard showed no real movement on compensation. The package on the table offers raises of 1% per year, climbing to 11% from 10% over a 4-year contract. That averages 2.75% per year, well below inflation. When the bargaining committee asked why Harvard offered only $1 million more in compensation while the endowment grew by $3.7 billion this past year, a Harvard lawyer stared at a calculator app and sat in silence. On pay equity between TFs and RAs, the committee asked why Harvard TFs are paid nearly 60% less than TFs at MIT. A top GSAS administrator responded: 'Maybe TFs at MIT work more.'
articleSummaries.7: Harvard indicated it is considering the union's Real Recourse proposal to make grievances available for remedies. Under that proposal, if a worker receives an unsatisfactory outcome from a Title IX, discrimination, or harassment case, there would be a contractual process to seek a better remedy. Harvard's lawyers said they were looking into the legal details.
articleSummaries.13: No movement on non-citizen worker rights since the union's 4/20 counter, nearly a month earlier. Harvard has not engaged with the union's immigration leave proposal, even though the University implemented a similar policy during COVID for workers detained or stranded abroad. On ICE-off-campus language, Harvard said 'we can't do that,' refusing to put constitutionally-afforded protections into the contract, even as peer institutions Yale, the UC system, and WPI have passed similar language.
articleSummaries.FA: Harvard's package would eliminate union-administered benefits across the board: healthcare, emergency funds, dental, legal expense, non-citizen worker assistance, childcare, and dependent premiums. The proposal also reverts 11 open articles to old contract language, and demands union concessions on 16 articles, many of them worse than the previous contract.
articleSummaries.19: The package proposal includes an erosion of fair processes for discipline and discharge.
articleSummaries.21: The package proposal would eliminate guaranteed health insurance during medical leaves.
articleSummaries.22: Harvard's package includes the elimination of the union-administered childcare benefit. It's listed among the union-administered benefits that would be cut entirely (alongside healthcare, emergency funds, dental, legal expense, non-citizen worker assistance, and dependent premiums).
articleSummaries.24: Harvard's package includes the elimination of the union-administered legal expense fund. It's listed among the union-administered benefits that would be cut entirely.
articleSummaries.30: Harvard's package includes the elimination of the union-administered emergency fund. It's listed among the union-administered benefits that would be cut entirely.
articleSummaries.33: Harvard's package would eliminate fair-share fees, the standard arrangement that ensures everyone who benefits from the contract contributes to sustaining the union.
articleSummaries.18: Harvard's package would reduce union access to worker orientations.

sessions.title: First Session After Strike
sessions.tldr: Harvard proposed raises below inflation and the elimination of union-administered benefit funds, but showed some movement at the table. Union reasserted proposals for an independent grievance procedure.

articleSummaries.20: There was some movement on compensation, but the offered raise still falls under inflation. The proposal ignores three things: workers received no raise in 2025-26, the wide pay gap between TFs and RAs goes unaddressed, and the offer trails what graduate workers at peer institutions are paid today. By 2029, TFs under this proposal would still qualify for SNAP food benefits. Harvard called the 1% raise over 4 years 'generous,' noting it would cost the University $1 million, which is less than 0.01% of the $10.2 billion flexible endowment. Hourly wages saw no movement at all: Harvard is still offering $0.50/year, while the union has been clear the floor needs to rise from $21.50 to $25/hour.
articleSummaries.21: Mentioned in the broader benefits discussion. Harvard's proposed increases to dental subsidies and parental support are a step forward, including broader eligibility, but these remain extracontractual programs Harvard can modify unilaterally without worker input.
articleSummaries.22: Harvard offered $6,500 per year per child. The union's prior coverage was $16,000 per child, and Harvard's own childcare facilities cost $3,780 per month, so the proposed amount doesn't cover two months of Harvard's own program.
articleSummaries.23: Harvard's benefits proposal continues to leave nearly 1,000 workers out: hourly workers, many Master's students, and DDes, EdLD, DrPH, and SJD candidates.
articleSummaries.24: Harvard proposed a subsidized MetLife legal services plan and suggested it would help with immigration needs. The plan materials show it doesn't cover urgent, time-sensitive immigration representation — the kind of rapid-response help non-citizen workers need when work authorization is at risk. It also appears not to cover representation in Title IX cases. Legal counsel often costs $40,000 or more, and Harvard's proposal eliminates the existing union legal support that made representation affordable.
articleSummaries.30: Folded into the broader benefits restructuring. Under Harvard's proposal, union-administered emergency funds would be replaced by University-administered alternatives that carry no contractual obligation to pay out.
articleSummaries.13: Tied to the legal services discussion. The MetLife plan Harvard proposed does not provide rapid-response immigration representation — exactly what non-citizen workers need to maintain visa and work authorization status while completing their degrees.
articleSummaries.7: The union reasserted its proposals for an independent grievance procedure offering real recourse to workers facing harassment, discrimination, and bullying.
articleSummaries.FA: Harvard proposed eliminating union-administered benefit funds entirely and replacing them with a 'new' University-administered structure. Much of that 'new' structure already exists as extracontractual programs (the Vivian B. Allen fund, GSAS family benefits, school-based emergency funds) being repackaged as if they were won at the bargaining table. Under the proposal, Harvard would not be contractually obligated to pay out a single penny from these funds, and disputes over fund access would be excluded from the grievance process. Roughly 1,000 workers would be cut out altogether: hourly workers, many Master's students, and DDes, EdLD, DrPH, and SJD candidates. Distributing benefits across multiple schools, separate funds, and administrators without clear eligibility rules, timelines, transparency, or appeals process creates bureaucratic obstacles right when workers — especially parents with monthly childcare expenses — most need help.

sessions.title: Update under strike threat (covers 4/9 + 4/13)
sessions.tldr: Most movement seen in over a year of bargaining. Article 27 (Holidays) reached TA. Harvard still refuses on core protections. Key fights ongoing on discipline, retaliation, harassment, health and safety.

articleSummaries.27: Tentative Agreement reached on 4/9 — the second TA of the bargaining cycle.
articleSummaries.19: Harvard's proposal would create a faster, weaker disciplinary process that lets the University discipline workers without an investigation, leaving workers to challenge discipline only after it's been imposed. The union pushed back on the absence of investigation, due process, and clear union representation rights.
articleSummaries.3: Harvard finally responded to demands about late appointment letters, but the counter still puts too much risk on workers. Late letters can leave workers without rent money. The union made clear that administrative failures shouldn't cost workers their paychecks, and that promised appointments should come with job security.
articleSummaries.6: Harvard showed partial movement on the grievance procedure, though no real engagement on the core issues.
articleSummaries.7: Harvard returned an article that restored some protections from the previous contract: rights to union representation, and limits on University pressure to settle informally instead of filing formal complaints. But Harvard still refused codified identity-specific protections and access to the union grievance process, both of which are standard across graduate union contracts.
articleSummaries.8: The union pushed harder for stronger anti-retaliation protections so workers can file grievances without fear. The union argued for a clear definition of retaliation workers can rely on, rather than vague assurances.
articleSummaries.10: The union presented a new proposal strengthening timelines and accountability around accommodations, building in protections for workers in mental health crises, and pushing Harvard to provide real care for wellness checks instead of defaulting to police.
articleSummaries.4: The union reasserted protections for workers whose appointments are cut or canceled, including RA protections and transition support.
articleSummaries.18: The union narrowed its access proposal while continuing to fight for union orientations, space, access, and resources to organize more effectively across campuses.
articleSummaries.AF: The union reasserted its academic freedom proposal. Harvard continues to refuse real contract language on academic freedom, even though it directly affects working conditions. Other graduate worker contracts already include this protection.
articleSummaries.16: The union reasserted Workload to bring management back into the conversation. Harvard has not yet responded to the union's workload concerns.

sessions.title: Session #21: No Money, No ICE Protections, and No Protections against Harassment & Discrimination
sessions.tldr: 21 sessions in, 62 hours at the table. Harvard reasserted positions on multiple articles, asked union to withdraw proposals, called a living wage 'unreasonable.'

articleSummaries.20: Harvard called the union's living wage proposal 'unreasonable' — even as RAs and TFs at MIT, Stanford, and Princeton earn substantially more from universities with smaller endowments. For higher G-year workers in humanities and social sciences paid entirely through teaching at roughly $26,000/year, Harvard considered the ability to make ends meet a 'financial aid issue' — which the University controls but refuses to bargain over. Harvard told the bargaining committee that TFs should 'look into getting jobs in the summer' and work 4-5 sections if they needed the money.
articleSummaries.13: Harvard said it views protections against ICE as something that would interfere with their 'relationship with the federal government,' despite other universities (including the University of California) offering similar provisions for nearly a decade. Harvard said they are unwilling to provide more monetary support or contract provisions because they believe they're doing enough already.
articleSummaries.7: Harvard maintains that its harassment and discrimination system works fine, despite hearing directly from four survivors at the previous session and the many instances of sexual violence and discriminatory conduct workers leave unreported because they fear Harvard's entirely internal procedures.
articleSummaries.9: Harvard handed the union a copy of the union's own Article 9 proposal without responding to it — one of several articles Harvard has never substantively engaged on.
articleSummaries.10: Same pattern: Harvard handed back the union's own Article 10 proposal without responding to it.
articleSummaries.18: Same pattern: Harvard handed back the union's own Article 18 proposal without responding to it.

sessions.title: Session #20: How much does a TF cost?
sessions.tldr: Heard a dozen-plus membership testimonies. Harvard rejected pay equity between TFs and RAs, refused to counter on non-citizen rights despite promising to (9 months overdue), passed token articles on Training and Job Posting.

articleSummaries.20: Harvard's counter offered raises below inflation and refused pay equity between TFs and RAs. The first-year offer is effectively the same money workers make today. The proposed 2.5% annual increases over 4 years would shrink real wages each year. After four semesters of top-up and summer funding run out, many workers earn just $26,000 teaching the standard load. Under Harvard's proposal, those workers would reach $29,000 by 2029 — still qualifying for SNAP in MA. When pressed, Harvard responded that 'no other contract has a 74% raise' and that 'this Union has agreed to the current pay structure before.' When reminded of testimony about TF precarity, Harvard asked 'how many in-unit workers in the liberal arts are even taking more than five years to graduate?' — though it's common knowledge, including from Harvard's own documentation, that liberal arts PhDs typically take around seven years.
articleSummaries.13: Harvard had committed at the previous session to bring a counter on non-citizen worker rights. They didn't. The union has been waiting nine months for movement on Article 13, and Harvard continues to arrive at each session without a counter.
articleSummaries.33: The union reasserted its proposal for fair-share fees so the union can sustain organizing financially.
articleSummaries.11: Harvard passed a short proposal on Training described as 'housekeeping changes' — neither party had signaled interest in revisiting this article.
articleSummaries.5: Harvard passed a short proposal on Job Posting described as 'housekeeping changes' — neither party had signaled interest in revisiting this article either.

sessions.title: Session #19: Everything's on the Table
sessions.tldr: All union proposals now on the table including economic demands. $55K base wage proposal. Expanded benefit funds. New articles on Lab Transition Program and Accessible Transit.

articleSummaries.20: The union put forward its compensation proposal: $55,000 base rate, $25/hour floor for hourly workers, and automatic annual increases of 5% or inflation — whichever is higher — for all student workers. After the 2021 Living Wage campaign moved the stipend to about $50K, that figure equals only $40K in 2021 dollars, meaning workers have taken a real pay cut. The proposal also fights for TF/RA pay equity: most TFs after the G4 year in Humanities and Social Sciences earn just $26,000 teaching the standard load, which qualifies them for food stamps in MA. Almost no other peer institutions use Harvard's classification system, which treats TFs as adjuncts paid by the section rather than as regular salaried workers.
articleSummaries.21: The union proposed fully-funded dental coverage and an expanded healthcare fund.
articleSummaries.22: The union proposed an expanded childcare fund.
articleSummaries.23: As part of the broader benefits proposal, the union called for expanded eligibility — including fixing gaps that currently lock out hourly workers, and making salaried workers eligible for the entire fiscal year in which they worked.
articleSummaries.24: The union proposed an expanded legal expense fund covering immigration, housing, tax, and workplace matters. Legal counsel often runs $40,000 or more, and existing union legal support has made representation accessible.
articleSummaries.30: The union proposed an expanded emergency grant fund. Workers are delaying care, paying out of pocket, taking on debt for legal or immigration costs, and scrambling when emergencies hit.
articleSummaries.7: The union reasserted its proposal for stronger harassment and discrimination protections, including access to the union grievance process for redress — a standard protection across graduate union contracts. Data shows 1 in 5 student workers has experienced harassment, discrimination, or bullying in their workplace. Harvard has rejected this proposal and taken away protections from the previous contract — including the right to union representation in meetings — so workers' only path to recourse runs through processes Harvard fully controls.
articleSummaries.LTP: The union proposed a new Transitional Support Program so RAs can leave unsafe, abusive, or broken advising relationships without losing pay or benefits. It would provide up to six months of guaranteed funding, tuition coverage, healthcare, and full benefits, with support starting quickly. The proposal is modeled on a similar program at MIT.
articleSummaries.AT: The union proposed guaranteed, reliable accessible transportation for workers approved for disability accommodations through the Daytime Van Service. The proposal expands access to both daytime and evening vans across all Harvard campuses and adds ride-share coverage when van wait times exceed 30 minutes.
articleSummaries.BFR: The union proposed rules for administering benefit funds across the contract — covering eligibility, timelines, and accessibility.
articleSummaries.BT: Included as part of the broader restructuring of benefit administration.
articleSummaries.FA: The union proposed expanding overall benefit fund access — moving the funds from $2.75M to $3.6M and broadening eligibility across the unit.

sessions.title: Session #18: First TA Won
sessions.tldr: Article 15 (Workspace) TA'd — first TA of the cycle. Harvard still ghosting on non-citizen protections (242 days). Health & Safety counter. Appointment letter counter dodges late-pay accountability.

articleSummaries.15: First Tentative Agreement of the cycle. Harvard agreed to provide available private space 'reasonably close' to the workplace for workers to hold office hours, supervisor meetings, and similar. At the table, 'reasonable' was clarified as generally under a 10-minute walk and generally on the same campus.
articleSummaries.13: The union pressed Harvard again after more than 8 months without any counter to the proposal — even as non-citizen workers face escalating risks. Harvard acknowledged they've been discussing Article 13 behind closed doors but still had nothing in writing. The union walked Harvard through the proposal again and made clear that non-citizen and international workers need enforceable protections now, not vague promises later.
articleSummaries.10: The union put another counter on the table with stronger, enforceable protections — clearer timelines for disability accommodations and safer approaches to wellness checks that don't default to armed responses. Harvard's response was the usual: 'that'll be difficult.'
articleSummaries.3: Harvard's counter added a line about pay being 'taxable income' but didn't address the real problem of late appointment letters and late pay. The University routinely sends letters late or promises jobs that don't materialize, and workers pay the cost through delayed pay and instability. The union submitted an RFI to the University in August 2025 to get hard data on these issues. The University is legally required to respond to RFIs, but is ghosting the union instead.
articleSummaries.6: The union's counter moved on grievance timelines to keep negotiations moving — down to 45 business days, still longer than the current contract. The union is still pushing for stronger, practical protections against retaliation when workers file grievances; Harvard is resisting.

sessions.title: Session #16: Slow but Steady
sessions.tldr: Counters received on employment letters, workspace access, and grievance/arbitration. Harvard cut grievance timeline from 80 business days to 35; refused codified privacy protections. Productive conversation on harassment protections.

articleSummaries.3: The union continued pressing Harvard to provide solutions for workers whose paychecks have been delayed by long processing times for employment appointments. Timely appointment letters are the mechanism that ensures workers get paid on time.
articleSummaries.15: The union was glad to see the University adopt the union's proposal guaranteeing private space for meetings related to teaching and research. The union is still seeking clearer language to ensure those spaces are genuinely accessible — not across campus — and that workers know how to reserve them in advance through a booking system.
articleSummaries.6: The University continues to deny the union's request for a more reasonable grievance filing timeline. The union's 80-business-day proposal was cut down to 35. Workers often don't realize their rights have been violated until weeks later. The University also continues to refuse codified privacy protections for workers in the grievance process.
articleSummaries.7: Productive conversation on strengthening protections for workers experiencing discrimination, harassment, or bullying. The union asked Harvard for multiple, flexible options for seeking redress: filing a grievance through the union, using the University's internal process, or pursuing both — either simultaneously or sequentially. The University remains insistent on limiting workers to one process only (their internal one), a one-size-fits-all approach that doesn't reflect the complexity of these situations and can change at any point with no input from the union.

sessions.title: Session #15: Membership reminds Harvard of our priorities
sessions.tldr: After 12 rejections at the prior session, BC delivered 10 counters in rapid succession. Productive conversation on academic retaliation. Harvard added 'or retaliation' language to Article 7.

articleSummaries.4: Among the ten counters the union returned after Harvard's 11/7 rejections — pushing Harvard to accept security pay for all teaching assignments beyond the 'guaranteed' teaching offered in fellowship packages.
articleSummaries.21: Among the ten counters — pushing Harvard to accept healthcare during leaves of absence.
articleSummaries.AF: Among the ten counters — pushing Harvard to accept academic freedom on matters relevant to the subject and purpose of workers' appointments.
articleSummaries.27: Among the ten counters — pushing Harvard to accept paid vacation days for all workers, accrued by month.
articleSummaries.7: Harvard returned a small but meaningful counter on Article 7. The new proposal sprinkled the phrase 'or retaliation' in several places — an optimistic signal that they recognize the union cannot rely on the 'Harvard ethos' alone to protect workers from harassment or retaliation. Academic retaliation is a real feature of Harvard's culture toward student workers.

sessions.title: Session #14: Getting access to health care is too radical for Harvard
sessions.tldr: Sat down with Harvard CFO for finance overview. Despite 11.9% gain on $56.9B endowment, no plans to address hiring freezes, layoffs, stagnant wages. Harvard rejected 12 of our proposed articles outright.

articleSummaries.26: Harvard rejected the union's proposals for paid family and medical leave (up to 12 weeks) and access to healthcare during leaves so no one loses coverage in a crisis.
articleSummaries.21: Harvard rejected the union's proposal for healthcare during leaves of absence.
articleSummaries.27: Harvard rejected the union's proposal for more than one personal day off per semester.
articleSummaries.4: Harvard rejected the union's proposal for full compensation for RAs and TFs whose appointments are canceled at the last minute.
articleSummaries.7: Harvard rejected the union's proposal for real recourse on harassment, discrimination, and bullying.
articleSummaries.8: Harvard rejected the union's proposal for real recourse on academic retaliation.
articleSummaries.AF: Harvard rejected any academic freedom protections that would let workers speak without fear in the classroom.

sessions.title: Session #13: We're still waiting
sessions.tldr: Harvard invited their Disability Resources director for an overview but couldn't provide data on denied accommodations. Union pushed on grievance timeline (one semester) and ungraded 'placeholder' credits during leaves.

articleSummaries.6: The union presented a counterproposal calling to extend the grievance filing timeline to roughly one semester, so workers have time to navigate the process fairly. Harvard offered only 5 extra days (bringing the total to 35) and refused to codify any commitment to accepting late grievances, claiming extensions could be granted case-by-case through 'mutual agreement.'
articleSummaries.26: The union pushed for guarantees that workers on leave retain student status, campus access, and health insurance — basic protections peer universities like Brown and Yale already provide. Harvard rejected the union's idea of ungraded 'placeholder' credits that would let workers on leave maintain enrollment, implying it would 'reward' those not making academic progress. Workers on leave for medical or mental health emergencies currently lose their health insurance precisely when they need it most.
articleSummaries.27: The union called for TFs to receive vacation time, proposing just one day per month. Harvard dismissed this, implying TFs' schedules are already 'flexible' enough.
articleSummaries.10: Harvard invited Kate Upatham, Senior Director of Disability Resources, to give an overview of the accommodations process. When the union asked about timing for accommodation requests and data on denied requests or informal resolutions, Harvard said this data is not readily available — despite many disabled workers expressing strong concerns with how the process has worked.

sessions.title: Session #12: Fruitful conversation, but still waiting for counters
sessions.tldr: Productive on grievance timeline (80 days), retaliation protections, union security. Harvard dismissed retaliation definition as 'too broad' and 'outside their control.' 16 articles brought; only 6 counters received.

articleSummaries.6: Harvard opened with clarifying questions on Article 6. The union emphasized the need to extend the filing timeline from 30 to 90 business days (about a semester), so workers aren't forced into rushed decisions. The union also pushed for stronger privacy protections and clearer anti-retaliation language. While Harvard expressed openness to better training for administrators about retaliation, they dismissed the union's proposed definition of retaliation as 'too broad' and 'outside their control.' Harvard says the University's 'ethos' is already non-retaliatory while refusing to put clear protections into policy or point to a working definition in the current contract.
articleSummaries.33: The union introduced a counter-proposal for agency-shop, ensuring everyone who benefits from the contract contributes through dues or a fair-share fee.
articleSummaries.16: Harvard asked clarifying questions on Workload but did not respond with a counter.
articleSummaries.15: Harvard asked clarifying questions on Workspace. The union underscored that all workers need dedicated desk space on campus to do their jobs.
articleSummaries.26: Harvard asked clarifying questions on Leaves. The union underscored that workers need continued access to healthcare during leaves — so no one loses coverage in a crisis — and that non-citizen workers shouldn't be left without visas.
articleSummaries.10: Harvard asked clarifying questions on Health and Safety. The union underscored that workers need timely and reasonable accommodations for disabilities, and safe workplaces free from violence, including protection from involuntary police entry into non-public spaces where workers live and work.

sessions.title: Session #11: We demand protection from academic retaliation
sessions.tldr: Director of new CSNDR briefed on Title IX. Harvard dodged real engagement on harassment/discrimination protections. Discussion got heated on union security; Harvard dismissed HUCTW comparison.

articleSummaries.7: Harvard invited Nicole Merhill, Director of the newly-formed CSNDR, to outline the University's existing Title IX policies. The union hoped this would open the door to real discussion of proposals for stronger protections — including grievability for discrimination and harassment cases and robust non-retaliation measures. Instead, Harvard dodged the union's questions and refused to engage with their own objections to the proposals, blocking the path toward a collaborative agreement. This leaves workers without real recourse beyond Harvard's internal system, where the University controls the process from start to finish.
articleSummaries.4: The union continued pressing for employment security: TFs should receive full pay if their sections are canceled, and at least two weeks' notice if that happens. Harvard's responses so far have not addressed these core issues.
articleSummaries.8: The union continued pressing for academic retaliation protections — no graduate worker should face retaliation from faculty mentors or advisors through recommendation letters, professional opportunities, or academic endeavors. Harvard's responses so far have not addressed these core issues.
articleSummaries.33: Discussion got heated. The union is fighting for a fair-share arrangement so everyone who benefits from the contract contributes to sustaining the union. Other Harvard unions (HUCTW) already operate under this system. When the union raised that, Harvard dismissed the comparison and suggested graduate workers are 'different' from other employees because they enter the University as students. Harvard insists it wants to treat campus unions equally but refuses to start by accepting the fair-share proposal.

sessions.title: Sessions #9 & #10 (double feature): The Big One
sessions.tldr: Harvard's carve-out scheme for ~1000 lab-science RAs. Union passed six major articles including the new Academic Freedom proposal. Harvard had nothing to pass.

articleSummaries.7: On 8/21, the union passed a counter on Non-Discrimination, Harassment, and Abuse — one of six articles passed at the session, reflecting the highest non-fiscal priorities of the unit according to the previous year's bargaining survey.
articleSummaries.9: On 8/21, the union passed a counter on Intellectual Property, Scholarly, and Research Misconduct.
articleSummaries.10: On 8/21, the union passed a counter on Health and Safety.
articleSummaries.19: On 8/21, the union passed its initial proposal on Discipline and Discharge.
articleSummaries.26: On 8/21, the union passed a counter on Leave Provisions.
articleSummaries.AF: On 8/21, the union passed its new Academic Freedom proposal.
articleSummaries.3: On 7/11, the union passed a counter on Employee Appointment Letters.
articleSummaries.8: On 7/11, when commenting on the Academic Retaliation article, Harvard asked why the union wanted to enshrine a neutral, non-University-run process for retaliation cases when the University has its own internal system. When the union explained the current process was insufficient for members, a Harvard representative asked: 'Well how do you know it's not working? To my knowledge there's been very little use?' The union's response: reporting misconduct to a board of the accused's colleagues tends to suppress reporting.

sessions.title: Session #8: We push for agency shop, real recourse!
sessions.tldr: Union proposed agency-shop for stronger union finances. Harvard refused to discuss Real Recourse, called the topic 'too contentious.' Harvard failed to offer guidance on non-citizens stranded abroad after visa revocations.

articleSummaries.33: The union proposed making HGSU an agency-shop union, where everyone who receives the benefits and protections of union advocacy contributes financially through membership dues or an equivalent fair-share fee. Agency shop is standard for most graduate unions in the US and would maintain the freedom to choose union membership while ensuring HGSU can keep advocating for improved wages, benefits, and protections long-term.
articleSummaries.7: Harvard refused to discuss Real Recourse on harassment, calling the topic 'too contentious.'
articleSummaries.9: Harvard resisted most of the union's clarifying questions about Harvard's proposed cuts to Intellectual Property protections.
articleSummaries.13: Harvard offered no guidance for non-citizen workers stranded abroad after visa revocations, and told the bargaining team they were 'being unfair' for asking.
articleSummaries.3: The union received a counterproposal from Harvard on appointment letters.

sessions.title: Session #7: Harvard ignores Real Recourse / Non-Discrimination and Employment Security
sessions.tldr: Harvard's lead negotiator delivered a 'State of the University' on financial instability. Counter-proposed on Article 7 (Non-Discrimination) that eroded protections from current contract. Article 27 (Holidays) proposal.

articleSummaries.7: Harvard's counter not only ignored the union's membership-approved Real Recourse proposal — it completely rejected current contract language, walking back agreements from the previous contract. Nearly every section of Harvard's counter-proposal defers to University policies that 'may be amended' at Harvard's will at any time. They cut out explicit language protecting specific groups including race, color, religion, caste, creed, sex, sexual orientation, and others — all currently in the previous contract. By defaulting to University-wide policies instead, Harvard is refusing to protect any group according to specific needs or concerns in the contract.
articleSummaries.4: Harvard claimed the union's initial Appointment Security proposal did 'a disservice to prior efforts' during the 2021 round of bargaining — because the union disagreed with their reading of who is eligible for security pay.
articleSummaries.27: The union presented its Holidays proposal — pushing for Spring Break leave for all student workers, requirements that employers inform workers about entitlement to personal time and holidays, and expanded eligibility for time off to all workers, including hourly positions.

sessions.title: Session #6: Harvard Owes us $400k in Legal Funds, Demands 'Please Say Thank You'
sessions.tldr: Powerful testimonies from non-citizen workers under constant threat. Harvard's lead negotiator yelled at the team about not being 'thankful,' had to be intervened on by a Provost. Refused to release $400K owed in legal funds.

articleSummaries.13: Several student workers testified powerfully about their lives: constant threat of being abducted from labs, classrooms, and homes; worry about being unable to finish their research if they travel; fear of returning home to countries hostile to their research. The need for legal counsel is immediate and expensive — tens of thousands of dollars per student. The union presented its Article 13 proposal, asking for comprehensive legal assistance in the event of detention or federal immigration enforcement, expanded leave and remote-work provisions for immigration proceedings, and protections against federal presence on campus or requests for records. As the union began presenting the relevant testimonies, Harvard tried to cut the team off and demanded the union proceed to another article. The union insisted on presenting four testimonies from the non-citizen worker community.
articleSummaries.18: The union presented its Union Access and Rights proposal, aimed at securing space, time, and finances for the union's administrative work. Asks include updated information sharing about workers in the unit, consistent union representation in worker orientations, dedicated ADA-compliant union workspaces across the Harvard campus, and a set of paid positions for workers who dedicate job-equivalent hours leading and organizing the union (such as HGSU executive board members, who currently volunteer uncompensated).
articleSummaries.24: Four years ago, the union won a contract provision for $100K/year to fund work-related legal expenses, such as the immigration threats workers currently face. Harvard has failed to properly release these funds, leaving the union unable to access nearly $400K that could help protect non-citizen workers right now. The union asked Harvard to make these contractually-owed funds accessible. Harvard's lead negotiator accused the bargaining team of not being 'thankful' for Harvard's legal efforts against Trump, accused a bargaining member of 'whitewashing,' and yelled at the team to a point where a University provost had to step in and intervene. The lead negotiator refused to engage further on the legal defense fund, calling it 'not relevant' to the current contract negotiations.

sessions.title: Session #5: Legal defense fund, Workload, and Harvard's many questions
sessions.tldr: Harvard again refused Zoom bargaining. Didn't fully address non-citizen protections or recent funding cuts. Extensive procedural questions on grievance and appointment letters. Union proposed Article 16 (Workload).

articleSummaries.16: The union proposed Article 16 on Workload. The article addresses a pervasive issue where some students teach without appropriate pay despite performing the same job and labor as their paid peers. The goal is to ensure all workers teaching are given appropriate job assignments and matching pay.
articleSummaries.13: The union followed up on questions about non-citizen protections. Harvard couldn't say how graduate student positions would be affected by recent federal funding cuts, but said they would get back to the union.
articleSummaries.24: The union raised concerns about Harvard's continued resistance to properly administering the legal defense fund won in the last contract, and discussed how understaffing at the Harvard Representation Initiative (HRI) has limited workers' access to legal services.
articleSummaries.6: Harvard asked extensive procedural questions about Article 6. The union emphasized the importance of longer timelines for workers to file a grievance. Harvard claimed extended timelines weren't 'standard' for other unions (though other examples of extended timelines exist) and expressed concern that students could 'forget details' about their workplace issue complaints.
articleSummaries.3: Harvard asked questions about Article 3. They expressed confusion about how little information student workers receive about tax withholding. When asked about sending out timely appointment letters with basic information like department/program, tax rate, and funding source, Harvard claimed it would be 'cumbersome and onerous' to do so, and blamed individual departments or programs for falling behind.

sessions.title: Session #4: Real recourse, funding cuts, and non-citizen safety
sessions.tldr: Three articles proposed: Employment Security, Non-Discrimination/Harassment/Abuse, and Academic Retaliation. Harvard had no immediate answers on funding cuts, DHS information sharing, or ICE presence on campus.

articleSummaries.4: The union presented its Employment Security proposal — aimed at securing better protections and rights for workers across a variety of appointments.
articleSummaries.7: The union presented its proposal on Article 7, taking a 'real recourse' approach to harassment, discrimination, abuse, and intimidation through choice, clarity, and care. Harvard pushed back, asserting that a roughly 10% dismissal rate for complaints in recent years is 'negligible.' The University also did not acknowledge how existing processes are highly time-restricted and often lead to arbitrary complaint dismissals.
articleSummaries.8: The union presented its Academic Retaliation proposal, with improved protections against academic retaliation.
articleSummaries.13: Harvard had no immediate answers about student worker funding security in the face of federal funding cuts, about the nature of information shared with DHS to remain SEVP-compliant, or about ICE presence on campus.

sessions.title: Session #3: Our first contract proposals & Bargaining Portal is up!
sessions.tldr: First contract proposals brought: Articles 3 (Appointment Letters), 6 (Grievance & Arbitration), 15 (Workspace). Harvard passed Article 9 (Intellectual Property).

articleSummaries.3: The union presented its first proposal on Appointment Letters.
articleSummaries.6: The union presented its first proposal on Grievance and Arbitration.
articleSummaries.15: The union presented its first proposal on Workspace, Remote Work, and Materials.
articleSummaries.9: Harvard's bargaining team passed a proposal on Article 9 (Intellectual Property, Scholarly, and Research Misconduct).

sessions.title: Session #2: Harvard Refuses Open Bargaining and Denies Protections Against ICE
sessions.tldr: Harvard rejected open bargaining proposals (despite 1200+ signature petition). Denied ICE/DHS protections during bargaining sessions. Union will bargain without ground rules.

articleSummaries.X: Despite delivering a petition for open bargaining with over 1,200 signatures and direct quotes from workers and community members, Harvard again rejected all of the union's proposed ground rules. The union proposed a compromise — bargaining observers would only be present on a muted Zoom webinar. In response to every proposal the union made, Harvard cut out all of the union's language around transparent bargaining. The University said it had a problem specifically with 'our unit' being able to observe negotiations.
articleSummaries.13: Harvard refused the union's requests to protect workers against ICE and other federal agents during bargaining sessions. The union asked Harvard to (1) notify HGSU if the University was informed of ICE presence and (2) enforce key-card access to limit potential ICE entry. Harvard rejected these in ground rules and refused to even verbally agree to any of these actions. When a committee member tried to explain the importance of a safe bargaining room, the University's lead negotiator cut them off, saying: 'You've talked an awful lot.' Harvard directed the union to its Office for General Counsel guidelines, which don't provide material protection against detention or deportation, and said: 'That policy is our policy.'

sessions.title: Session #1: Harvard Rejects Open Bargaining
sessions.tldr: First bargaining session. University rejected open bargaining, safety/accessibility, and reasonable accommodations proposals, except for one specific disability accommodation.

articleSummaries.X: Two weeks after sending Harvard the union's proposed ground rules, the University rejected the proposals — which included a plan for open bargaining (both in-person and on Zoom) and a request for protections from ICE and other law enforcement during bargaining. Harvard accepted one specific proposed disability accommodation needed for the bargaining committee to participate in in-person negotiations. During the session, Harvard claimed observers would unfairly 'pressure them,' and that open bargaining in 2021 had caused a 'chilling effect' on some members of the Harvard legal team.
